topics.title: The Bible alone?
topics.objection: Christians should believe only what is in the Bible (sola scriptura). Tradition is man-made.
answer: The Catholic Church holds that Scripture is the inspired word of God and the supreme written norm of faith, and also that God’s word reaches us in two linked ways: Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition. Both flow from the same source and are interpreted by the Church’s teaching office, the Magisterium, which serves the word and does not stand above it (Dei Verbum 10).

The Bible itself does not teach that it alone is the rule. Paul tells the Thessalonians to hold fast to the traditions they were taught “by word of mouth or by letter” (2 Thessalonians 2:15), and calls the Church, not a book, “the pillar and bulwark of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15). The New Testament books were written, collected and recognised as Scripture within the Church, and the list of books (the canon) is not itself a verse of Scripture. Second Timothy 3:16 says Scripture is useful for teaching and for equipping the man of God; it does not say it is the only authority.
Catholics do not treat Tradition as adding new doctrines, but as the living handing on of what the apostles received, in worship, creeds and teaching.

topics.title: Why do Catholic Bibles have 73 books?
topics.objection: The Catholic Bible adds books to the Bible, the “Apocrypha”.
answer: The Old Testament in Catholic Bibles includes seven books (Tobit, Judith, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch) and parts of Esther and Daniel that Protestants often leave out. These were in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) that the first Christians, writing in Greek, mostly used and quoted. They were recognised as Scripture by the Church in the fourth and fifth centuries (the councils of Hippo, 393, and Carthage, 397, and the letter of Pope Innocent I, 405), and again at the Council of Florence and the Council of Trent.

The shorter Hebrew canon fixed by Jewish teachers after the time of the apostles was not the Bible of the early Church; it was Luther in the sixteenth century who removed these books from the Old Testament. The New Testament contains allusions to some of them (for example Hebrews 11:35 and 2 Maccabees 7), and the practice of praying for the dead has a basis in 2 Maccabees 12:44-46. Catholics do not “add” books: the Church received 46 Old Testament and 27 New Testament books as the canon, and no one is able to point to a verse that lists the books of the Bible.

topics.title: Did Jesus found a Church with authority?
topics.objection: Jesus never founded an institution; the Church is a human invention.
answer: Jesus chose twelve apostles, gave them a share in his own authority (“Whoever listens to you listens to me”, Luke 10:16), the power to bind and loose (Matthew 18:18) and the Great Commission to teach and baptise all nations (Matthew 28:18-20). He promised that “the gates of hell shall not prevail” against his Church (Matthew 16:18) and that the Spirit of truth would guide the apostles into all truth (John 16:13).

The Acts of the Apostles shows this structure at work: Matthias replaces Judas (Acts 1:15-26), the apostles settle a doctrinal dispute at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15), and Paul appoints elders (Acts 14:23, Titus 1:5). The Catholic Church teaches that the bishops are the successors of the apostles, and that the bishop of Rome, the Pope, is the successor of Peter. It also teaches that the Church’s authority is a service to the truth, for Christ is its head.

topics.title: Is Peter the rock? The papacy
topics.objection: Peter was not the first Pope. The rock in Matthew 16 is Peter’s faith, or Christ himself.
answer: Jesus gives Simon a new name, Cephas (Aramaic for rock, Greek Petros), and says, “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church… I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:18-19). The “keys” echo Isaiah 22:22, where the royal steward holds the keys of David’s house and “shall open, and none shall shut”: an office with successors, not just a person. Jesus also prays that Peter’s faith will not fail and tells him to strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:31-32), and charges him three times to “feed my sheep” (John 21:15-17).

In Acts, Peter leads the choice of a replacement for Judas, preaches on Pentecost, and speaks first at the Council of Jerusalem. His name heads every list of the apostles. The Church has understood from earliest times that the bishop of Rome, where Peter died, inherits this ministry of unity: the Catechism says the Pope is “the perpetual and visible source and foundation of the unity both of the bishops and of the whole company of the faithful” (CCC 882). The Church also teaches that the Pope is infallible only when he solemnly defines a doctrine on faith or morals for the whole Church, not in everything he says.

topics.title: The Trinity
topics.objection: The Trinity is not in the Bible; it is a pagan idea or a contradiction.
answer: Catholics worship one God in three Persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, equal in being and distinct as Persons. The word “Trinity” is not in the Bible, any more than “Bible” is, but the teaching is. The Old Testament insists that God is one (Deuteronomy 6:4); the New Testament shows the Father, the Son and the Spirit each called God and acting together: at Jesus’ baptism (Matthew 3:16-17), in the baptismal formula “in the name (singular) of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19), and in Paul’s blessing (2 Corinthians 13:13).

The Church put this in words at the Councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) to answer those who denied that the Son is truly God. It is a mystery, which means that we cannot fully understand it, but it is not a contradiction: God is one in nature (what He is) and three in Persons (who He is). It is not saying 1 = 3. The Trinity is also at the heart of how Christians pray: “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

topics.title: Is Jesus God?
topics.objection: Jesus never claimed to be God; that was invented later.
answer: The Gospels show Jesus claiming what only God can claim. He forgives sins (Mark 2:5-7), is Lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28), and says “before Abraham was, I AM” (John 8:58), using the divine name from Exodus 3:14; his listeners picked up stones to kill him for blasphemy. He says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and accepts Thomas’ confession, “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28). John’s Gospel begins, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God… and the Word became flesh” (John 1:1, 14), and Paul says that in Christ “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9).

The Church teaches that Jesus is one Divine Person with two natures, truly God and truly man, as the Council of Chalcedon (451) put it. His miracles, and above all his resurrection, are the signs given to confirm who he is.

topics.title: Did Jesus really rise from the dead?
topics.objection: The resurrection is a myth, or the disciples hallucinated.
answer: The earliest written testimony is Paul’s creed in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, which he “received” (so it is older than the letter, written about AD 55): Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred at once (most of whom were still alive), James, and last of all to Paul. The Gospels agree that women found the tomb empty, an unlikely detail to invent in a world where a woman’s testimony counted for little. The disciples, who had run away at the arrest, became fearless witnesses who suffered and died rather than deny what they had seen.

A resurrection is not the resuscitation of a corpse: the risen Jesus has a transformed, glorified body that can pass through closed doors but also eats fish and shows his wounds. It is a historical event with a meaning beyond history, which is why Paul says, “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). The Catechism calls it “the crowning truth of our faith in Christ.”

topics.title: Mother of God
topics.objection: Calling Mary the Mother of God means she is older than God, or a goddess.
answer: “Mother of God” (Theotokos, “God-bearer”) was defined at the Council of Ephesus (431), and it is a statement about Jesus before it is a statement about Mary. Mary is the mother of Jesus, and Jesus is a divine Person. Mary is not the source of his divinity, which is eternal, but she gave him his human nature, and a mother is the mother of a whole person, not of part of one. Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, called her “the mother of my Lord” (Luke 1:43), and “Lord” is the title the Old Testament uses for God.
To deny the title is to suggest that the child in the womb was not God yet. That is why the Church insisted on it: it guards the truth that Jesus is God made man.

topics.title: The Immaculate Conception
topics.objection: Mary was a sinner like everyone else; the Immaculate Conception is not in the Bible.
answer: The Immaculate Conception does not mean that Jesus was conceived without a human father (that is the virginal conception). It means that Mary herself, from the first moment of her existence, was preserved by God from original sin by a grace given in view of the merits of her Son (defined by Pope Pius IX in 1854). She was redeemed in the most perfect way: kept from falling, not lifted out afterward.

The Church finds the root of this in Scripture’s pattern: the angel greets Mary as “full of grace” (Luke 1:28), a title in place of her name, and the Ark of the Covenant, which carried God’s word, was made pure and holy. Eve was without sin before the Fall; Mary, the “new Eve”, was called to be the mother of the Redeemer, and the early Fathers contrasted “Eve’s disobedience” with “Mary’s obedience”. Romans 3:23 (“all have sinned”) allows exceptions in context: Jesus did not sin, and infants and the severely disabled cannot personally sin.

topics.title: The Assumption of Mary
topics.objection: The Assumption is not in the Bible and was invented in 1950.
answer: The Church teaches that Mary, at the end of her earthly life, was taken body and soul into heavenly glory. It was defined in 1950, but the belief is much older: the feast of her “Dormition” (falling asleep) was celebrated in the East by the sixth century, and no city in the ancient world claims her relics, though cities claimed those of many other saints.

Scripture does not describe it, but supports its fittingness. Enoch and Elijah were taken up (Genesis 5:24, 2 Kings 2:11); the Ark of the Covenant, which was God’s dwelling, was brought to rest in the Temple (Psalm 132:8, 2 Chronicles 5:7), and Revelation 11:19-12:1 moves from the Ark appearing in the heavenly Temple to “a woman clothed with the sun”. The Church sees in Mary a preview of what awaits all the faithful: the resurrection of the body.

topics.title: Was Mary always a virgin?
topics.objection: The Bible speaks of the “brothers” of Jesus, so Mary had other children.
answer: The Church teaches that Mary was a virgin before, during and after the birth of Jesus (CCC 499). In the Bible the Greek word for brother, adelphos, is used broadly, as the Hebrew “ach” is, for cousins and kinsmen: Lot is called Abraham’s “brother” though he is his nephew (Genesis 14:14, 16). The Gospels name “James and Joses” as sons of another Mary who stood at the cross (Matthew 27:56), not of Mary of Nazareth. At the cross Jesus entrusts his mother to John (John 19:26-27), which would be unnecessary if she had other sons to care for her.

Mary’s question at the Annunciation, “How can this be, since I have no husband?” (Luke 1:34), has long been read as showing a decision to remain a virgin. The Fathers and the Reformers (including Luther and Zwingli) held this teaching.

topics.title: Praying to the saints
topics.objection: Praying to saints is worship of the dead, and Jesus is the only mediator.
answer: Catholics do not worship saints; worship (latria) belongs to God alone. We ask the saints to pray for us, just as we ask living friends to pray for us. Paul asks the Romans to “strive together with me in your prayers” (Romans 15:30), and James says that “the prayer of a righteous person has great power” (James 5:16). The saints in heaven are not dead: God “is not God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32), and Jesus speaks with Moses and Elijah at the Transfiguration.

Paul’s “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5) is spoken in the very passage where he urges prayers for everyone (2:1-4). Christ is the one Mediator of redemption; asking someone to pray with us does not replace his mediation but shares in it, as members of his Body. Revelation shows the saints in heaven offering our prayers to God (Revelation 5:8; 6:9-10). The Church says, “Being more closely united to Christ, those who dwell in heaven fix the whole Church more firmly in holiness” (CCC 956).

topics.title: The Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist
topics.objection: The bread and wine are only symbols of Jesus’ body and blood.
answer: Catholics believe that at Mass, by the power of the Holy Spirit and the words of the priest, the bread and wine become the Body and Blood, Soul and Divinity of Christ (the Church calls this transubstantiation: the appearance of bread and wine remains, while what they truly are changes). Jesus said, “This is my body… this is my blood” (Matthew 26:26-28), not “this represents”. In John 6 he says, “unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you” (6:53), and when many disciples left because “this is a hard saying”, he did not soften it or call after them to say he was speaking in a figure (6:60-66). The verb he uses for “eat” changes in John 6:54 to a word meaning to chew or gnaw.

Paul warns that whoever eats and drinks unworthily “will be guilty of profaning the body and blood of the Lord” and “eats and drinks judgement on himself” (1 Corinthians 11:27-29), which would make no sense if it were only a symbol. The earliest Christian writers, such as Ignatius of Antioch (about AD 107) and Justin Martyr (about 155), say plainly that the Eucharist is the flesh of Jesus Christ.

topics.title: Is the Mass a sacrifice?
topics.objection: Christ’s sacrifice was once for all, so the Mass cannot repeat it.
answer: The Church agrees that Christ died once for all (Hebrews 9:26-28; 10:10-14), and the Mass does not repeat or add to that sacrifice. It makes the one sacrifice of Calvary present for us, as the Passover meal made the Exodus present to each generation. At the Last Supper, Jesus took the bread and wine and said, “This is my body, which is given for you… this is my blood… poured out for you”, in the language of sacrifice and covenant. The Church’s worship in Revelation shows a “Lamb standing as though slain” in the heavenly liturgy (Revelation 5:6).

Malachi foretold a “pure offering” in every place from the rising to the setting of the sun (Malachi 1:11), which the earliest Christians (for example the Didache, about AD 100) saw fulfilled in the Eucharist. The priest acts in the person of Christ; the sacrifice is Christ’s own, and we join our lives to his.

topics.title: Confession to a priest
topics.objection: Only God can forgive sins; we do not need to confess to a man.
answer: Only God forgives sins, and in Jesus God has given this power to men. On Easter evening Jesus breathes on the apostles and says, “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained” (John 20:22-23). A priest would not be able to “retain” a sin unless he first knew it, which implies that the sins are named. Jesus had already shown that “the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins” (Mark 2:10), and the crowd praised God for giving “such authority to men” (Matthew 9:8). Paul speaks of the “ministry of reconciliation” given to the apostles (2 Corinthians 5:18-20), and James tells the sick to call the elders, and to “confess your sins to one another” (James 5:14-16).

In the sacrament of Penance the priest acts in the person of Christ. The penitent’s sorrow, confession, penance and the priest’s absolution together express and bring about God’s forgiveness. The seal of confession is absolute: a priest may never reveal anything he hears.

topics.title: Baptising babies
topics.objection: Baptism requires faith, so babies should not be baptised.
answer: Baptism is God’s gift, not a human achievement. The New Testament speaks of whole households being baptised (Acts 16:15, 33; 1 Corinthians 1:16), and the word “household” in that time included children. Peter said on Pentecost, “the promise is for you and for your children” (Acts 2:38-39). Baptism takes the place of circumcision (Colossians 2:11-12), which was given to boys at eight days old. Jesus said, “Let the children come to me” (Matthew 19:14).

The faith of the Church, parents and godparents supports the child until he or she can profess it personally. The Church baptises infants because original sin affects every person, and because grace is a free gift. Christians have baptised infants from the earliest times: Origen (about 248) said the Church received this tradition from the apostles.

topics.title: Does baptism save?
topics.objection: We are saved by faith alone; baptism is only a symbol.
answer: The New Testament speaks of baptism in very strong terms. Jesus says, “unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). Peter says, “Repent, and be baptised… for the forgiveness of your sins” (Acts 2:38), and, “baptism… now saves you” (1 Peter 3:21). Ananias tells Paul, “Rise and be baptised and wash away your sins” (Acts 22:16), and Paul says we are saved “by the washing of regeneration and renewal in the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5). Baptism is not a symbol only: through it God washes away original sin and all personal sin, gives new life in Christ and makes us members of his Church.

This is not “works salvation”: the baptised do nothing; they receive. The Church teaches that God is not bound by his sacraments, and that those who die for Christ without baptism (baptism of blood) or who seek God sincerely and would have been baptised had they known (baptism of desire) can be saved.

topics.title: Priestly celibacy
topics.objection: Priests should marry. The Bible says a bishop should be the husband of one wife.
answer: Celibacy for priests in the Latin Church is a discipline, not a doctrine, and it has exceptions: some Eastern Catholic Churches have married priests, and married Protestant clergy who become Catholic may be ordained. Jesus and Paul were both unmarried. Jesus said some “have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to receive this receive it” (Matthew 19:12), and Paul says the unmarried man is “anxious about the things of the Lord” and has an undivided heart (1 Corinthians 7:32-35). “The husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2) forbids a second marriage; it does not command marriage.

The Church asks its priests, who are called to give themselves entirely to God’s people, to live as Christ did, as a sign of the life to come, when “they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30).

topics.title: Why only men as priests?
topics.objection: The male priesthood is discrimination.
answer: The Church teaches that she has no authority to ordain women to the priesthood (John Paul II, Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, 1994). It is not a judgement on women’s dignity or ability. Jesus, who treated women with great respect and had women disciples, chose twelve men as apostles, though it went against some of the customs of his day, and the apostles in turn appointed men as their successors. Mary, the greatest of the saints, was not an apostle. In the early Church, there were many women saints, prophets and teachers (Priscilla, Phoebe, Junia), and women have been Doctors of the Church, but none were ordained priests.

The priest acts “in the person of Christ the Bridegroom” toward the Church, his Bride, which is why the sign of a man is fitting. Women and men are equal in dignity but have different roles, as the Church sees it.

topics.title: Purgatory
topics.objection: Purgatory is not in the Bible. Christ’s sacrifice is enough.
answer: Purgatory is the final purification of those who die in God’s grace and friendship but are not yet fully cleansed, so that they may enter the joy of heaven. Paul describes a person whose work is burned yet “he himself will be saved, but only as through fire”.

Praying for the dead is an ancient Jewish and Christian practice (2 Maccabees 12:44-46), and it makes sense only if the dead can still be helped. Jesus speaks of sins forgiven “in the age to come” (Matthew 12:32) and of a prison from which one does not come out “till you have paid the last penny” (Matthew 5:25-26). The word “purgatory” is not in the Bible, but the Church’s tradition, from the early inscriptions of the catacombs to Saint Augustine, includes prayers for the dead. Christ’s sacrifice is fully sufficient; purgatory is about being made able to receive it fully.

topics.title: Sunday or Saturday?
topics.objection: The Bible says the Sabbath is Saturday; Catholics changed it.
answer: The Church keeps Sunday as the Lord’s Day because Jesus rose from the dead on “the first day of the week” (Mark 16:2, 9; John 20:1) and appeared to the disciples on the following Sunday (John 20:26). Paul says that no one should judge Christians “in questions of food and drink or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a sabbath” (Colossians 2:16-17), and the Council of Jerusalem did not require Gentile believers to keep the Mosaic law (Acts 15). The idea that the Catholic Church “changed” the day in the fourth century is not historically accurate: Sunday worship is attested already in Ignatius and Justin Martyr in the second century. topics.title: Marriage, divorce and annulment
topics.objection: The Church bans divorce, and annulment is “Catholic divorce”.
answer: Jesus taught that marriage is a lifelong union: “What God has joined together, let not man put asunder” (Mark 10:2-12; Matthew 19:3-9). A valid sacramental marriage between baptised persons cannot be dissolved by any human power. The Church can recognise that a marriage which looked valid never truly existed because something essential was lacking from the beginning, such as free consent, or the intention to be faithful, or the ability to carry out the commitment of marriage. Civil divorce is sometimes tolerated for protection, but remarriage after divorce while the first spouse is alive is not possible for Catholics, since “whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery” (Luke 16:18). Divorced Catholics who have not remarried remain full members of the Church, and those who have remarried can still take part in the life of the Church in many ways.

topics.title: Contraception
topics.objection: The Church’s ban on contraception is out of date.

The Bible condemns the deliberate frustrating of conception in Onan’s case (Genesis 38:9-10), although scholars debate the main point of that story. The tradition, from the Fathers, taught that contraception is wrong. Humanae Vitae predicted social consequences, which many see in today’s culture. topics.title: Faith, science and evolution
topics.objection: Science has disproved the Bible; Genesis contradicts evolution.
answer: The Church teaches that faith and reason cannot contradict each other, since the same God is the author of both (CCC 159). Genesis does not teach how the heavens go, but how one goes to heaven (as Galileo quoted Cardinal Baronius). Genesis 1-3 teaches in the language of its time, with a literary structure of days and a garden, that God created everything out of nothing and called it good, that human beings are made in his image, and that sin entered the world through a free choice. The Church does not require anyone to believe in a six-day creation or a young earth.

The Church has not condemned evolution as a scientific theory. Pope Pius XII (Humani Generis, 1950) allowed it as a matter for discussion, and Pope John Paul II said it was “more than a hypothesis” (1996), while insisting that the human soul is created directly by God. The Big Bang theory was first proposed by a Catholic priest, Georges Lemaître. The Church’s teaching is that the universe has a Creator, and human beings have a spiritual soul.

topics.title: Why does God allow suffering?
topics.objection: If God is good and all-powerful, why is there evil and suffering?
answer: The Catechism says plainly that there is no quick answer: “Only Christian faith as a whole constitutes the answer to this question” (CCC 309). God made a world “in a state of journeying” and gave free will to angels and humans, and with it the possibility of moral evil. He permits evil only because he can bring a greater good from it, as with the cross, the worst evil in history, which became the source of our salvation. The Book of Job shows that God does not give a neat explanation for the suffering of the innocent, but meets Job in person.

Christians do not say suffering is good in itself. Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35), healed the sick, and promised that God “will wipe away every tear” (Revelation 21:4). He also shares our suffering: on the cross God entered the worst we suffer. Paul says our sufferings can be joined to Christ’s for the good of others (Colossians 1:24) and that “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8:28).

When Judas fell, the Eleven chose a successor so that “another may take his office” (Acts 1:20-26). The laying on of hands carried a real gift (2 Timothy 1:6).

The early Church counted bishops in lists reaching back to the apostles: Clement of Rome and Ignatius of Antioch write of the apostles appointing overseers and of unity around the bishop, and Irenaeus appeals to the succession of bishops as a guarantee of true teaching. The Catholic Church holds that this unbroken line preserves the apostolic faith (CCC 861-862). The royal priesthood of all baptised believers (1 Peter 2:9) is real, and is distinct from the ministerial priesthood that serves it.

topics.title: Development of doctrine
topics.objection: Catholics keep adding new doctrines that the apostles never taught.
answer: The Church says she cannot add to the deposit of faith, which closed with the apostles. What develops is our understanding of it. topics.title: Can we trust the Gospels?
topics.objection: The Gospels were written long after Jesus by unknown authors, so they are legends.
answer: The Church teaches that the four Gospels are historical: they “faithfully hand on what Jesus the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation” (Dei Verbum 19; CCC 126). Luke says that he followed everything closely from the beginning and had the accounts of “eyewitnesses and ministers of the word” (Luke 1:1-4). Paul quotes an even earlier creed about the death, burial, and resurrection of Jesus, which he received from others within a few years of the events (1 Corinthians 15:3-8).

The Gospels were written within about thirty to sixty years of the events, which is very close by the standards of ancient history. They preserve embarrassing details, such as the disciples’ failures and the women as the first witnesses. The evangelists selected and arranged their material for theological purposes, so they differ in detail, but they agree on the core: Jesus’ ministry, death, and resurrection.

topics.title: The virgin birth
topics.objection: The virgin birth was borrowed from pagan myths, and Isaiah 7:14 only says “young woman”.
answer: Matthew and Luke each say that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary without a human father (Matthew 1:18-25; Luke 1:34-35). They tell the story independently and in different ways, which suggests an early tradition. Matthew cites Isaiah 7:14, “the virgin shall conceive,” as fulfilled. The Hebrew word almah means a young woman of marriageable age, and the Jewish translators of the Greek Septuagint, some two centuries before Christ, rendered it parthenos, “virgin.” Matthew follows that reading.

The pagan stories of gods coupling with women are not parallels: here there is no marriage of God and a woman, but a creative act of the Holy Spirit. The virginal conception shows that Jesus’ sonship is a gift of God and not a human achievement, and that the new creation begins with God’s initiative (CCC 496-499, 503).

topics.title: Fully God and fully man
topics.objection: Jesus is either God or man, and cannot be both. The Church’s language is philosophy, not Scripture.
answer: The Gospel of John says that “the Word was God” and that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14). Paul writes that Christ, “though he was in the form of God,” took the form of a servant and was born in human likeness (Philippians 2:6-8). The Council of Chalcedon (AD 451) summed this up: one person, the Son of God, in two natures, divine and human, “without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.”

Because Christ is truly God, his sacrifice has infinite value, and because he is truly man, he can die and represent us (Hebrews 2:14-17; 4:15). He had a human body, a human soul, a human will, and grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52), and he still has all that he is as God. The Church stresses both sides because losing either one destroys the Gospel (CCC 464-469).

topics.title: Old Testament prophecies of Christ
topics.objection: Christians read Jesus into the Old Testament. The prophecies are about other things.
answer: The New Testament does not claim every Old Testament line was a straight prediction. It claims that the story, the law, the temple, and the prophets all point forward to Christ, and that he fulfils them. Isaiah’s Suffering Servant, who “was wounded for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:5), is cited in the New Testament by Philip with the Ethiopian (Acts 8:32-35). Psalm 22, which begins with the words Jesus uttered on the Cross (Matthew 27:46), describes pierced hands and feet and the division of garments.

Micah 5:2 names Bethlehem as the origin of the ruler, and Zechariah 9:9 describes the king riding a donkey. Jesus himself explained “in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:27). The Church teaches that the Old Testament has its own value as revelation, and that it is fully understood only in Christ (CCC 128-130, 601, 702-716).

topics.title: Why did Jesus have to die?
topics.objection: A loving God would forgive without needing a bloody sacrifice.
answer: The Church teaches that Christ died “for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3), and that in his Passion he freely offered himself in love as a sacrifice to the Father for our redemption (CCC 606-618). Sin is a real offence against God and wounds human nature, and love’s answer to it is costly. “Greater love has no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). The Cross is not the Father punishing an unwilling Son, but the Father and the Son, in the Spirit, acting together to rescue sinners.

Scripture uses many pictures for what Jesus did: ransom (Mark 10:45), Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), sin offering (Hebrews 10:10-14), and victory over death (Colossians 2:14-15). They fit together in the Church’s teaching that Christ, who is both God and man, could offer to God the perfect satisfaction that humanity owed and could not give.

topics.title: The Rapture and the end times
topics.objection: Believers will be secretly taken up before a seven-year tribulation (the Rapture).
answer: The Rapture is a nineteenth-century idea and is not found in the earliest Christian teaching. The Catholic Church reads 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17, “we who are alive… shall be caught up together with them in the clouds,” as describing the public return of Christ, with a trumpet and a shout, at the general resurrection. Jesus says that his coming will be like lightning that flashes from east to west (Matthew 24:27), and not hidden.

The Catechism teaches that before Christ’s return the Church will pass through a final trial that shakes the faith of many (CCC 675), and that no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36). The book of Revelation is read by the Church as a vision of Christ’s victory in history and at the end of time, not as a timetable. Believers are told to stay awake and ready rather than to predict dates.

topics.title: The book of Revelation, 666 and the 144,000
topics.objection: Revelation says only 144,000 will be saved, and 666 refers to the Pope or to a microchip.
answer: The 144,000 in Revelation 7 and 14 is a symbolic number: twelve tribes times twelve apostles times a thousand, which stands for the full people of God. Just after the 144,000 are sealed, John sees “a great multitude which no man could number, from every nation” (Revelation 7:9), which is the same people in a different image. The number 666 is explained in the text itself: “it is the number of a man” (Revelation 13:18), usually taken to refer to Nero Caesar, whose name, written in Hebrew letters, adds up to 666 (some manuscripts have 616, which fits the Latin spelling of Nero).

Revelation is apocalyptic writing, filled with symbols from the Old Testament, to console persecuted Christians in the first century and to assure them that Christ, the slain Lamb, has already won. Catholics read it in the Liturgy, where the Mass echoes the heavenly worship of Revelation 4-5. Attempts to match its images to a modern politician or technology have failed again and again (CCC 675-677).

topics.title: Transubstantiation
topics.objection: The word “transubstantiation” isn’t in the Bible, and the Eucharist is a symbol.
answer: The word is the Church’s way of expressing what Jesus said: “This is my body… this is my blood” (Matthew 26:26-28). Paul says that those who eat and drink unworthily are “guilty of profaning the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:27) and that the cup is a participation in the blood of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16). The Church teaches that the substance of bread and wine is changed into the substance of Christ’s body and blood, while the appearances (taste, colour, texture) remain the same (CCC 1376-1377). The change is called transubstantiation.

“Substance” here is the philosophical term for what a thing is at its deepest level, as opposed to its outward properties. It was chosen to say clearly what the Church had always believed, and to exclude readings that make the Eucharist only a symbol or that suppose a physical, cannibalistic change. Christ is present whole and entire, body and blood, soul and divinity, under each form.

topics.title: Why only Catholics receive Communion
topics.objection: Closed communion is exclusive and unloving.
answer: Receiving Communion is a public sign of full communion in the same faith, sacraments, and governance. Paul says that those who share the one bread are one body (1 Corinthians 10:16-17) and warns that eating “in an unworthy manner” brings judgment (1 Corinthians 11:27-29). The earliest description of the Eucharist outside the New Testament, by Justin Martyr, says that no one may take part unless they believe the teaching is true and have been baptised.

The Catholic Church does not judge anyone’s heart or deny that other Christians have real faith and grace. But because a person who receives affirms the Church’s faith about the Eucharist, the Church asks that Catholics be in a state of grace, having fasted one hour, and that non-Catholics not receive except in rare cases of grave need (CCC 1395, 1400-1401, 1415). Others are welcome to come forward for a blessing.

verses.why: We who are many are one body

The apostles’ teaching and the breaking of bread
One Lord, one faith, one baptism

topics.title: Eucharistic adoration
topics.objection: Worshipping a piece of bread is idolatry.
answer: Catholics adore the Eucharist because they believe that, after consecration, the bread is no longer bread but Christ himself. If that is true, the right response is the one given to Christ throughout the Gospels: the magi “fell down and worshiped him” (Matthew 2:11), the disciples worshipped the risen Jesus (Matthew 28:9, 17), and Thomas called him “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28). If it were not true, adoration would be idolatry. The question is whether Jesus is really there.

The Church teaches that Christ remains present in the consecrated host as long as the appearances of bread last (CCC 1377), and that he is worthy of the worship due to God alone (CCC 1378-1381). Adoration is also a way of prolonging the grace of the Mass: Jesus’ question in Gethsemane, “Could you not watch with me one hour?” (Matthew 26:40), is lived out by many in an hour before the Blessed Sacrament.

verses.why: They fell down and worshiped him
My Lord and my God

topics.title: Anointing of the Sick
topics.objection: Last rites are a ritual for the dying with no scriptural basis.
answer: James writes: “Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders (presbyters) of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick man, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven” (James 5:14-15). The Church sees in this the sacrament of Anointing of the Sick. It also recalls that the Twelve “anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them” (Mark 6:13).

The sacrament is not only for the dying: it is for anyone seriously ill or elderly, and it can be received again if the illness worsens. It gives strength, peace, and courage, unites the sufferer to the Passion of Christ, and, if the person is unable to confess, forgives sins (CCC 1499-1532). When the person is near death, it is often given with confession and Viaticum (Holy Communion), which are together the “last rites.”

verses.why: Let him call for the elders… anointing him with oil

topics.title: Confirmation
topics.objection: Confirmation is a man-made rite. Baptism gives the Holy Spirit.
answer: Acts records an action after baptism that gave the Spirit through the apostles. In Samaria, Philip baptised the new believers, but the Holy Spirit “had not yet fallen on any of them.” So Peter and John came, “prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,” and “laid their hands on them” (Acts 8:14-17). Paul did the same at Ephesus (Acts 19:5-6). Hebrews lists “instruction about baptisms, the laying on of hands” among the basic teachings (Hebrews 6:2).

The Church teaches that Confirmation completes baptismal grace. It seals the baptised with the Spirit (Ephesians 1:13) and strengthens them to bear witness (CCC 1285, 1302-1305). The sign is anointing with chrism, a perfumed oil blessed by the bishop, with the words “Be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit.” In the West it is normally given by the bishop, to show the connection to the apostles.

verses.why: They laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit
The Holy Spirit came on them

topics.title: “Call no man your father”
topics.objection: Matthew 23:9 forbids Catholics from calling priests “Father”.
answer: Jesus says: “Call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven” (Matthew 23:9). Taken without context, that would also forbid calling your own dad “father,” and the New Testament does not read it that way. Jesus uses hyperbole in the same passage, and the point is against the vanity of those who seek titles (Matthew 23:5-12). Stephen addresses the Jewish elders as “brethren and fathers” (Acts 7:2), and Paul says, “I became your father in Christ Jesus through the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15).

Catholics call priests “Father” because they are spiritual fathers who give birth to the life of grace through the sacraments and teaching (CCC 1548, 1551). The same title has been used since the early Church for bishops. Jesus’ point, that all fatherhood comes from God (Ephesians 3:14-15), is exactly what Catholics hold.

verses.why: Call no man your father on earth
I became your father in Christ Jesus

topics.title: Grace and merit
topics.objection: Catholics try to earn their way to heaven. The Bible says salvation is a free gift.
answer: Catholic teaching begins with grace as a free, undeserved gift: “By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not your own doing, it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8). No one can merit the first grace of conversion (CCC 2010). The Council of Trent taught that our justification is by grace alone, and that no work before it earns it. The Catholic Church condemned the idea that a person can save himself.

But the Bible also speaks of rewards, of faith working through love (Galatians 5:6), and of God working in us “both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12-13). Because God gives us a share in his own life, our cooperation with grace can be rewarded, in the way a father delights in the gift a child gives with the father’s own money. This is what the Church means by merit, and it too is a gift of God (CCC 2006-2011, 1996-1999).

Work out your salvation, for God is at work in you
Faith working through love

topics.title: Predestination and free will
topics.objection: God predestines some to heaven and others to hell, so human choices don’t matter.
answer: Scripture says that God “chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4-5) and that those he foreknew he also predestined (Romans 8:29-30). The Catholic Church teaches that God has a plan of loving goodness for all, and that he wants all people to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4; CCC 1037, 1058). She rejects the idea of “double predestination,” in which God directly creates some people for hell: “God predestines no one to go to hell” (CCC 1037).

The Church also teaches that human beings have real freedom and are responsible for their actions (CCC 1730-1738). God’s knowledge of what we will freely do does not take our freedom away, because he does not know in time as we do. Jesus warns, invites, and judges as though our choices count, because they do (Matthew 7:13-14; 25:31-46).

verses.why: Those whom he foreknew he also predestined
He chose us in him before the foundation of the world

topics.title: Mortal and venial sin
topics.objection: All sins are equal in God’s eyes. The distinction between mortal and venial sin isn’t biblical.
answer: John writes: “If anyone sees his brother committing what is not a mortal sin, he will ask, and God will give him life… There is sin which is mortal… all wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin which is not mortal” (1 John 5:16-17). Jesus speaks of the “weightier matters of the law” (Matthew 23:23) and of greater and lesser sins (John 19:11), and Paul lists sins that keep one from the kingdom (1 Corinthians 6:9-10; Galatians 5:19-21). Not all sins break our friendship with God to the same degree.

The Church teaches that a sin is mortal when it is a grave matter, committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent (CCC 1857). It destroys charity in the heart and, unless repented, deprives us of eternal life. Venial sin weakens charity without breaking it, and is forgiven through prayer, the Eucharist, and works of love (CCC 1854-1863).

topics.title: Unbaptised babies and limbo
topics.objection: The Church teaches that babies who die without baptism go to hell.
answer: The Church has never taught that unbaptised infants go to hell. The Catechism says: “As regards children who have died without Baptism, the Church can only entrust them to the mercy of God, as she does in her funeral rites. Indeed, the great mercy of God who desires that all men should be saved, and Jesus’ tenderness toward children which caused him to say: ‘Let the children come to me, do not hinder them,’ allow us to hope that there is a way of salvation for children who have died without Baptism” (CCC 1261).

“Limbo” was a theological opinion, never a doctrine of the Church. In 2007 the International Theological Commission, with the approval of Pope Benedict XVI, concluded that there are serious grounds for hope that such children are saved. At the same time, the Church insists that we must not neglect to baptise infants (CCC 1250).

topics.title: What is heaven like?
topics.objection: Heaven is just clouds and harps, or we simply float around as spirits.
answer: The Church describes heaven as perfect, unending communion with the Trinity, Mary, the angels, and all the blessed (CCC 1024). Paul says that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard… what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9), and John speaks of seeing God “face to face” (1 John 3:2; 1 Corinthians 13:12). This is the “beatific vision,” the fulfilment of the human desire for truth and love.

The Christian hope is also not for escape from the body: at the Last Day the dead will be raised and heaven and earth will be renewed (Revelation 21:1-4; Romans 8:19-23). Jesus’ resurrection body could be touched, ate fish, and still passed through closed doors (Luke 24:39-43; John 20:19). Heaven is not boring: it is the full life for which we were made (CCC 1023-1029, 1042-1050).

verses.why: A new heaven and a new earth
Then face to face
We shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is

topics.title: Particular and final judgment
topics.objection: Nobody is judged until the end of the world, and Christians don’t get judged at all.
answer: Hebrews 9:27 says that “it is appointed for men to die once, and after that comes judgment.” The Church teaches two moments: the particular judgment, at the hour of death, when each soul receives its eternal destiny of heaven, purification, or damnation (CCC 1021-1022); and the general judgment at the return of Christ, when all will be raised and the secrets of hearts revealed (Matthew 25:31-46; John 5:28-29; CCC 1038-1041). Jesus tells of Lazarus and the rich man, in which the dead already face their reward or punishment (Luke 16:19-31).

Christians are not exempt: Paul says that “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10) and that believers’ works will be tested by fire (1 Corinthians 3:12-15). We are judged on love: the criteria in Matthew 25 are feeding the hungry, welcoming the stranger, and visiting the sick.

verses.why: After death comes judgment

topics.title: Praying for the dead
topics.objection: After death, our fate is sealed and prayers for the dead do nothing.
answer: Judas Maccabeus took up a collection to offer sacrifice for the fallen soldiers, “in view of the resurrection… it is a holy and pious thought. Therefore he made atonement for the dead, that they might be delivered from their sin” (2 Maccabees 12:43-45). The Jews at the time of Jesus prayed for the dead, and the practice is attested in Christian inscriptions, in the prayers of the early liturgies, and in Tertullian and Augustine, who mentions Monica’s request to be remembered at the altar.

Paul prays for Onesiphorus on “that day” (2 Timothy 1:16-18), which most naturally refers to the judgment after his death. Since the Church is one body in Christ, the living can help those being purified, and the saints help us (CCC 958, 1030-1032). Praying for the dead is an act of mercy, and it is a firm hope in the resurrection.

topics.title: Angels and guardian angels
topics.objection: Angels are folk tales, and praying to your guardian angel is unbiblical.
answer: Angels are spiritual, personal beings created by God, who serve him and help humanity (Hebrews 1:14). They appear throughout Scripture: Gabriel announces the births of John and Jesus (Luke 1:11-38), an angel strengthens Jesus in Gethsemane (Luke 22:43), and angels attended the empty tomb. The Church teaches that their existence is a truth of faith (CCC 328).

Jesus says of children, “their angels always behold the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10), which the Church’s tradition has read as pointing to a guardian angel for each person (CCC 336, quoting St Basil: “Beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd”). When the disciples hear Peter at the door after his release, they say, “It is his angel!” (Acts 12:15). Asking the help of our guardian angel is a form of asking for intercession, like asking a friend in the Church to pray for you.

verses.why: Their angels always behold the face of my Father
He will give his angels charge of you

topics.title: Relics and sacramentals
topics.objection: Honouring relics, holy water, and medals is superstition.
answer: The Bible shows God working through physical objects. A woman touched the fringe of Jesus’ cloak and was healed (Matthew 9:20-22). Handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched Paul healed the sick (Acts 19:11-12), and Peter’s shadow was hoped to heal (Acts 5:15). A dead man thrown into Elisha’s tomb came to life when his body touched Elisha’s bones (2 Kings 13:21). Catholics venerate relics (the bodies or belongings of saints) because the body is sacred, and God honours it.

Sacramentals are blessed objects and actions, such as holy water, ashes, candles, and medals, that prepare us to receive grace and help us sanctify daily life (CCC 1667-1673). They have no power of their own: they work through the prayer of the Church, and the faith of the user. The Church condemns superstition, which attributes magical power to the object itself (CCC 2111).

topics.title: Demons and exorcism
topics.objection: Exorcism is superstition. Demons are a medieval fiction.
answer: The Gospels report that Jesus often cast out demons and gave the Twelve and the seventy-two authority over them (Mark 1:23-27; 3:14-15; Luke 10:17-20). Jesus distinguishes illnesses from possession, and the Church does too. She teaches that the devil and other demons are fallen angels (CCC 391-395), that their power is limited, and that they cannot overcome those who rely on Christ.

The Church performs exorcisms of the sacramental kind in baptism (renouncing Satan), and the major exorcism of a possessed person only with the bishop’s permission and after medical and psychological causes are ruled out (CCC 1237, 1673). The ordinary Christian response to temptation is the one Jesus used in the desert: Scripture, prayer, and fasting (Matthew 4:1-11).

topics.title: Fasting, Lent and penance
topics.objection: Fasting is a Pharisee’s practice, and Christians are free from food rules.
answer: Jesus assumes that his disciples will fast: “When you fast…” (Matthew 6:16-18), and he says that “the days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast” (Matthew 9:15). He himself fasted for forty days before his ministry (Matthew 4:2). The early Church fasted before choosing leaders (Acts 13:2-3; 14:23), and the Didache (about AD 100) tells Christians to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays.

The forty days of Lent echo Moses on Sinai, Elijah on Horeb, and Jesus in the desert. The Church asks Catholics to fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, to abstain from meat on Fridays in Lent, and to do some penance on other Fridays (CCC 1434, 1438, 2043). The purpose is not to earn God’s love but to put the body and the appetites in order, to turn the heart back to God, and to share with the poor (Isaiah 58:6-7).

verses.why: When you fast, anoint your head
Then they will fast

topics.title: The death penalty
topics.objection: The Church has always approved of the death penalty, or the Church has changed its teaching.
answer: The Church’s long-standing teaching was that the state has the right to impose capital punishment when it is the only way to protect society. In 2018 Pope Francis changed paragraph 2267 of the Catechism to state that the death penalty is “inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,” and that the Church works with determination for its abolition. This is a development in the application of a principle: the sacredness of human life, which includes the guilty (Genesis 4:15; 9:6), and the modern ability to protect society without execution.

Scripture gives different signals. The Old Law prescribes death for many crimes (Genesis 9:6; Exodus 21:12), but God spares Cain (Genesis 4:15) and Jesus rescues the woman caught in adultery from stoning (John 8:1-11). Paul says the ruler “does not bear the sword in vain” (Romans 13:4). The Church today asks governments to use non-lethal means and to give the guilty time for repentance (CCC 2266-2267).

topics.title: Euthanasia and assisted suicide
topics.objection: People should have the right to die with dignity. Suffering is pointless.
answer: The Church teaches that every human life is a gift of God to be received, not a possession to be disposed of (Psalm 139:13-16; CCC 2258, 2280). Euthanasia, the direct and intentional ending of the life of a sick or dying person, and assisted suicide are morally unacceptable, even when requested, because they are choices to kill (CCC 2277). A patient may, however, refuse burdensome or disproportionate treatment, and pain may be relieved with drugs even if this shortens life, as long as death is not intended (CCC 2278-2279).

Suffering is not good in itself, but it is not meaningless: Christ redeemed it by his Passion, and we can unite our sufferings to his (Colossians 1:24). The Church asks for more compassion, not less, with palliative care, company, and the sacraments, so that no one feels like a burden.

topics.title: Same-sex attraction and marriage
topics.objection: The Church hates gay people and condemns who they are.
answer: The Church distinguishes between a person and an act. It teaches that persons with same-sex attractions “must be accepted with respect, compassion, and sensitivity. Every sign of unjust discrimination in their regard should be avoided” (CCC 2358). The attraction itself is not a sin. It also teaches that every person is called to chastity, and that sexual acts between persons of the same sex cannot be approved because they are not open to life and do not express the complementarity of man and woman (CCC 2357, 2359).

This rests on Scripture’s view of marriage and the body: “male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27; Matthew 19:4-6) and on passages that treat same-sex acts as sinful (Romans 1:26-27; 1 Corinthians 6:9-10; Leviticus 18:22). The same Church that holds this teaching also holds that all people are made in God’s image and loved by him. Many Catholics who experience same-sex attraction, living chastely, have described friendship, community, and prayer as central to their lives.

topics.title: Chastity and sex before marriage
topics.objection: Sex outside marriage is a private matter, and the Church’s rules are outdated.
answer: The Church teaches that sexual union is a total gift of self, which is why it belongs within the permanent, faithful, fruitful covenant of marriage. Jesus affirms the lifelong union of man and wife (Mark 10:6-9), and the New Testament repeatedly lists sexual immorality (porneia) among sins that exclude from the kingdom (1 Corinthians 6:9-11, 18-20; Hebrews 13:4). Paul says the body is “a temple of the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:19).

Chastity is a virtue for every state of life. For the married it means fidelity; for the unmarried, abstinence; for the vowed, celibacy (CCC 2337-2350). The Church recognises that this is hard and that people fail, which is why she offers confession and community, and she holds that sexual integrity is a good for personal freedom, not only a rule.

topics.title: In vitro fertilisation
topics.objection: Why does the Church oppose IVF? It helps couples have children.
answer: The Church understands the desire for a child as good (Genesis 30:1; 1 Samuel 1:10-11). It teaches that a child is “a gift” and not a right or a product (CCC 2378), and that the child should be the fruit of the spouses’ own loving union. IVF replaces that act with a laboratory procedure. It typically creates more embryos than are implanted, and many are frozen or destroyed, which the Church holds to be a grave violation of the dignity of human life from conception (CCC 2376-2377).

Treatments that help the marital act to achieve conception are permitted (CCC 2375), including some fertility-restoring medical care. The Church also reminds couples with infertility that they can have spiritual fruitfulness through adoption, service, and works of mercy, and she grieves with those who suffer this cross (CCC 2379).

topics.title: Adam and Eve, evolution and original sin
topics.objection: Science has disproved Adam and Eve, so original sin is a myth.
answer: The Church teaches that Genesis 1-3 uses figurative language to teach real truths: God created everything out of nothing, humanity is made in his image, man and woman are for each other, and a primeval sin entered the human story (CCC 337-342, 355-361, 390). It says nothing against the biological evolution of the human body, but holds that each human soul is created directly by God (Pius XII, Humani Generis; CCC 366). Catholics are free to believe in evolution, and not free to deny the soul, the original unity of the human race, or the fall.

Paul’s teaching on Adam as the head of the human race, through whom sin and death came, and Christ as the new Adam, is central (Romans 5:12-21; 1 Corinthians 15:21-22), and the Church has therefore not abandoned the idea of a real first human pair. How that fits with the details of paleoanthropology is a question for scientists and theologians, not settled by the Church.

topics.title: Should Genesis be read literally?
topics.objection: Catholics are either fundamentalists or they don’t believe the Bible.
answer: The Church teaches that the “literal sense” of a passage is what the human author intended to convey, which depends on its literary form (CCC 109-110). The Catholic tradition has read Genesis in several ways: Augustine wrote about the creation days as a literary structure, and Aquinas insisted that the faithful should not tie the faith to a particular scientific interpretation. The Pontifical Biblical Commission (1909) allowed that the days of Genesis need not be 24 hours.

Genesis 1 is a carefully structured account of God ordering the world as a temple and giving humanity its place. It teaches that the world is good, created by one God out of nothing, with the Sabbath as its goal. What the Church requires is that the central teachings be held: creation from nothing, the unity of the human race, the fall, and the creation of the soul by God (CCC 279-301, 355-379).

topics.title: Does the Bible support slavery?
topics.objection: The Bible condones slavery, so it can’t be trusted morally.
answer: Slavery existed in the ancient world, and the Old Testament law regulates it, with limits that were unusual for the time: Hebrew slaves were to be freed after six years (Exodus 21:2), kidnappers were put to death (Exodus 21:16), and runaways were not to be returned (Deuteronomy 23:15-16). The law does not ideally endorse it, and Jesus says of divorce that Moses allowed it “for your hardness of heart” (Matthew 19:8): the law is a stage in God’s teaching of a people.

In the New Testament Paul asks Philemon to receive his runaway slave Onesimus “no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 16), and he lists slave traders among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). Galatians 3:28 says “there is neither slave nor free… in Christ.” The Catechism teaches that slavery is a grave offence against human dignity (CCC 2414), and Popes Paul III, Gregory XVI, and Leo XIII condemned enslaving people. Christianity’s deeper principle of the equality of persons in the image of God led, over time, to abolition.

topics.title: Violence in the Old Testament
topics.objection: The God of the Old Testament commands genocide, and so cannot be the God of love in the New.
answer: The Church reads the Old Testament as a real revelation that is also incomplete. God teaches a people steeped in violent cultures step by step (CCC 53, 122), and some of the texts, like the conquest narratives in Joshua, are hard. The Church’s tradition offers several approaches: the commands may be partly hyperbolic ancient-war language (the “total destruction” texts in Joshua are followed by accounts in which the same peoples remain), they were limited in scope, and the Church Fathers (Origen, Augustine) also read them allegorically as the Christian’s struggle against sin.

The Old Testament also contains the commands to protect the stranger, widow, and orphan, and Hosea’s and Jonah’s portraits of God’s mercy. Jesus is the fullness of revelation (Hebrews 1:1-2), and the New Testament does not set God against God: the same God of love is the judge. Catholic scholars are open about the difficulty, and the Church does not teach that God commands anyone to kill the innocent today.

topics.title: The poor and social justice
topics.objection: Faith is a private matter. The Church should stay out of politics and economics.
answer: Jesus identifies himself with the poor: “As you did it to one of the least of these my brethren, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40). The prophets denounce the oppression of the poor (Amos 5:11-24; Isaiah 58:6-10), and James says that “faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead” (James 2:14-17). The Church’s social teaching, from Rerum Novarum (1891) to Laudato Si’ (2015), applies this to workers’ rights, the dignity of labour, the universal destination of goods, and care for creation.

The Church asks governments and individuals to give priority to the poor, a “preferential option” that does not exclude anyone (CCC 2443-2446). The works of mercy, corporal and spiritual, are the daily way each Christian responds (CCC 2447). The Church does not propose a political party, but insists that no political or economic system can treat the human person as a mere means.

topics.title: Other religions
topics.objection: All religions lead to the same God, or the Church condemns other religions.
answer: The Second Vatican Council taught that “the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy” in other religions, and regards their teachings with sincere respect, since they often reflect “a ray of that Truth which enlightens all men” (Nostra Aetate 2). At the same time, the Church insists that Christ is “the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6) and that the fullness of revelation is in him. She rejects the claim that all religions are equally true, since they contradict each other on basic matters, such as who Jesus is.

Judaism has a special place, as the Jews are the people of the first covenant, which God never revoked (Romans 9:4-5; 11:29; CCC 839-840), and Muslims, who worship the one God, are also mentioned (CCC 841). Respect and dialogue go with proclamation: Christ sent his Church to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19-20), and the Church does so without coercion.

topics.title: Does God exist?
topics.objection: There’s no evidence for God. Faith is belief without reason.
answer: The Church teaches that God can be known with certainty by the natural light of human reason from created things (Romans 1:19-20; Wisdom 13:1-9; CCC 31-36; Vatican I). Thomas Aquinas set out “five ways” of reasoning from the world to God: from motion, causation, contingency, degrees of perfection, and the order of the world. Many thinkers, believers and not, find the existence of a rationally ordered universe or of consciousness and moral obligation hard to explain without a source beyond it.

Faith is not blind: the Church calls it a free assent to God’s revelation, supported by reasons such as miracles and prophecy, but it goes beyond what reason alone can establish (CCC 156-159). “Faith and reason are like two wings,” John Paul II wrote in Fides et Ratio. The mysteries of faith, such as the Trinity, are above reason, not against it.

topics.title: If God is good, why is there evil?
topics.objection: A good and all-powerful God would not allow evil.
answer: The Church acknowledges that no short answer removes the problem (CCC 309). The Catechism’s reply is that God created a world “in a state of journeying” toward perfection, with real freedom for his creatures, including freedom to refuse him (CCC 310-311). God is not the cause of moral evil (CCC 311), but permits it, and brings greater goods out of it: “God would not allow evil if he did not draw good from evil itself” (CCC 311, citing Augustine). The supreme example is the Cross.

The Bible does not hide the pain: Job protests, the Psalms lament, and Jesus weeps and cries out on the Cross. God’s answer to Job is not an argument but a revelation of his wisdom and presence (Job 38-42), and the answer of the New Testament is that God enters suffering in Jesus. Paul adds that “the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed” (Romans 8:18). The final answer is promised: God “will wipe away every tear” (Revelation 21:4).

topics.title: Do miracles happen?
topics.objection: Miracles are impossible, so the Gospel miracles are legends.
answer: If God exists and created the laws of nature, it is not irrational to think he could act within them in unusual ways. The Church holds that Jesus’ miracles are “signs” that the kingdom of God has come (CCC 547-550), and that they invite faith and do not force it (CCC 548). The Gospels report that even Jesus’ opponents did not deny that he did extraordinary works: they claimed he did them by Beelzebul (Mark 3:22).

The Church is cautious about modern miracles. Lourdes keeps a medical bureau, and the Church requires documented, medically inexplicable cures for the canonisation of saints. The most important miracle is the resurrection, and the Church invites people to examine the evidence for it (1 Corinthians 15:3-8).

topics.title: Women in the Church
topics.objection: The Church is sexist, and Paul says women must be silent.
answer: Women are prominent in the Gospels and the Church: women follow and support Jesus (Luke 8:1-3), Mary Magdalene is the first witness of the resurrection (John 20:11-18), Phoebe is a deaconess (Romans 16:1), Priscilla teaches Apollos with her husband (Acts 18:26), and Junia is “prominent among the apostles” (Romans 16:7). Mary is the greatest of the saints, and of the 37 Doctors of the Church, four are women.

Paul’s texts on women keeping silent (1 Corinthians 14:34-35; 1 Timothy 2:11-15) are hard to interpret and must be read with his clear acceptance of women prophesying and praying in church (1 Corinthians 11:5). On the question of priesthood, the Church teaches that Christ chose only men as apostles and that she has no authority to change this (CCC 1577), which says nothing against women’s equal dignity, as shown by John Paul II’s teaching on the “feminine genius.”

topics.title: Money, tithing and the prosperity gospel
topics.objection: God wants Christians to be rich. Give to the church and receive back.
answer: Jesus warns that “you cannot serve God and mammon” (Matthew 6:24) and that “it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (Mark 10:25). The New Testament praises generosity (2 Corinthians 9:6-8) and describes the first Christians sharing what they had (Acts 2:44-45), but it does not promise earthly wealth. Paul calls the love of money “the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6:10). The saints and the Cross show that following Christ often costs.

Catholics are called to give to the Church and the poor (CCC 2043, 2446-2447), and to hold their possessions as stewards. Almsgiving, with prayer and fasting, is one of the three traditional works of Lent. The “prosperity gospel” turns the good news into a transaction, and it is at odds with Jesus’ words that his disciples should expect suffering for his sake (Matthew 5:10-12; Luke 9:23).

topics.title: Is the Hail Mary in the Bible?
topics.objection: Catholics pray to Mary and make up prayers that Scripture doesn’t contain.
answer: The first half of the Hail Mary is drawn directly from the Gospel of Luke: the angel Gabriel’s greeting, “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28), and Elizabeth’s words, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1:42). The second half, “Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death,” was added by the Church over the centuries, and expresses the request for intercession.

Asking Mary to pray for us is like asking any believer to pray for us, which Paul often does (Romans 15:30; Colossians 4:3). Catholics hold that those who have died in Christ are alive in him, and are still members of the same family, so they can pray for us (Luke 20:38; Hebrews 12:1; Revelation 5:8). The title “Mother of God” follows from the fact that Jesus is God (Luke 1:43; CCC 495).
